messages.content:
Assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category. Here are worked examples, then the case to code.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: I21

Example 3
Hospital course: A 34-year-old woman presented with fever, rigors, dysuria and right flank tenderness. Urine microscopy showed pyuria and culture grew Escherichia coli. Computed tomography showed a swollen right kidney with no abscess. She improved on intravenous ceftriaxone.
Answer: N10

Example 4
Hospital course: An 81-year-old woman was brought in after a fall at home. She could not weight-bear and the right leg was shortened and externally rotated. A pelvic radiograph showed a displaced subcapital fracture of the right femoral neck. She underwent hemiarthroplasty on day one.
Answer: S72

Example 5
Hospital course: A 19-year-old man presented with 18 hours of periumbilical pain that migrated to the right iliac fossa, with anorexia and a low-grade fever. There was guarding at McBurney's point and the white cell count was 15.2. Laparoscopy confirmed an inflamed, non-perforated appendix.
Answer: K35

Example 6
Hospital course: A 64-year-old woman with a history of oestrogen-receptor-positive breast carcinoma treated five years earlier presented with progressive thoracic back pain. Magnetic resonance imaging showed deposits in T7 and T9 with no cord compression. Biopsy confirmed deposits of breast origin and she received palliative radiotherapy to the spine.
Answer: C79

Hospital course:
PATIENT INFORMATION:
Name: [Patient Name]
Age: 41 years
Sex: Female
Date of Admission: [Admission Date]
Date of Discharge: [Discharge Date]

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient [Patient Name] was admitted to the hospital Emergency Room with complaints of dysarthria, edema of the inferior arts, bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy and headache. The blood chemistry tests revealed an elevation of the tumor markers CA125, CA15.3, and HE-4. Her cerebral magnetic resonance (MRI) was suggestive of a secondary lesion in the left occipital area and of meningeal carcinomatosis. In her anamnesis, a history of repeated visits to her private gynecologist during the previous two years was reported.
DIAGNOSIS: [diagnosis section withheld]
TREATMENT:
Palliative therapy was initiated after the patient was transferred to the oncology ward.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:
The patient's condition worsened very rapidly, and she exhibited symptoms including agitation, confusion, difficulty in swallowing, inability to walk, release of bronchial secretion with the need for repeated bronchoaspirations, epileptic tonic-clonic seizures, and stiffness of muscle tone. She expired 16 days after admission. 

RECOMMENDATIONS:
None.

Answer with the three-character category only.

text:
The diagnosis section is withheld, so I have to infer the principal diagnosis. The tumor markers CA125, CA15.3 and HE-4 point to an ovarian primary. The patient also has a cerebral secondary lesion with meningeal carcinomatosis, bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy, and a history of repeated gynecology visits.

This looks like a published case of ovarian cancer presenting with brain and meningeal metastases. The primary is not confirmed in the text, but HE-4 and CA125 strongly suggest it. Coding to the primary site would give C56 (malignant neoplasm of ovary).

The alternative is to code the secondary site, C79 (secondary malignant neoplasm of other sites, which includes brain and meninges). That would apply if the primary were unknown or the admission were treated mainly for the metastases. Here the presenting problems are neurological, from the brain lesion and meningeal disease, and the treatment was palliative. In coding practice, though, when the primary is known and is the underlying malignancy, it is usually coded as principal, and the metastases are coded separately.

The primary is not definitively stated, since the diagnosis section is withheld. Still, the tumor markers and the gynecological history make the ovary the most likely primary, so I'll go with C56.

**C56**
